intro: Kawazu sits on the east coast of the Izu Peninsula, and its two mapped trees stand about 600 metres apart, both reached from Kawazu Station. The great camphor of Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja is fifteen metres round, the last survivor of seven great camphors that once stood in the old district. Beside the Odoriko Onsen bathhouse, the Great Cycad of Shinmachi spreads four branches from a ten-metre trunk.
meta_description: Kawazu, Japan: a fifteen-metre camphor, last of the district's seven giants, and a Monument cycad near Kawazu Station.
question_meta: Kawazu's mapped tree is the great camphor of Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja, fifteen metres round and cited at a thousand years or more.
question_answer: Kawazu's oldest and only mapped tree is the great camphor of Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja, a Cinnamomum camphora standing behind and to the left of the main hall. It measures about fifteen metres round and twenty-four metres tall, and published sources put it at a thousand years or more.
question_context:
The thousand-year figure for the camphor is tradition rather than a ring count. The girth is not: the Environment Ministry's giant-tree survey recorded fourteen metres in 1990, when the tree ranked nineteenth nationally, and fifteen in 2001. Within Shizuoka it is tied for second. Its trunk has not hollowed, unlike the peninsula's other two famous camphors at Atami and Ito. It was designated a national Natural Monument in 1936, the last of seven great camphors the district was once known for.

About six hundred metres away, near the Odoriko Onsen Kaikan bathhouse, the Great Cycad of Shinmachi spreads four thick branches along the ground from a central trunk roughly ten metres tall, unusually tall for a cycad. The whole clump measures 7.76 metres around at the base, the combined mass of stem and limbs rather than one trunk's girth. Tradition places its age from six hundred to over a thousand years; it became a National Natural Monument in 1936, one of only ten individually designated cycads in Japan. Its vigour has declined somewhat in recent years.

faq.q: What is special about this tree?
faq.a: It is the last of the seven great camphors that once gave the old Kawazu district its name for them, and at roughly fifteen metres round it is tied for the second-thickest tree in Shizuoka prefecture.
Published sources agree on a thousand years or more. That is a traditional figure rather than a measured one; the girth, recorded twice by the national giant-tree survey, is the solid number.

faq.q: Which camphor is the monument tree?
faq.a: Not the two near the torii. The designated tree stands further in, behind and to the left of the main hall, and a sign at the entrance points the way.
Yes. It stands on the open grounds of Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja, also known as Kawazu Kinomiya Shrine.
Take the Izu Kyuko Line to Kawazu Station and walk about 12 to 15 minutes, or catch a bus from the station to the Kinomiyaguchi stop.

faq.q: What is Kawazu's other mapped tree?
faq.a: The Great Cycad of Shinmachi, about 600 metres from the camphor near the Odoriko Onsen Kaikan bathhouse. A National Natural Monument since 1936, one of only ten individually designated cycads in Japan, with four branches sprawling along the ground from a ten-metre central trunk.

trees.name: The Great Camphor of Sugihokowakenomikoto Shrine

location.address: 154 Tanaka, Kawazu, Kamo District, Shizuoka 413-0504, Japan (grounds of Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja, also called Kawazu Kinomiya Shrine, behind and to the left of the main hall)
location.neighbourhood: Kawazu, east coast of the Izu Peninsula

trees.story:
Six of the seven are gone. Old Kawazu district was known for the Kawazu-go Nanakakae Nanakusu, its seven great camphors, and by the middle of the Meiji era this was the only one left standing.

It is not the first camphor you meet. Two smaller ones grow near the torii of Sugihokowakenomikoto-jinja, the shrine locals call Kinomiya, and enough visitors have stopped at those that the shrine put up a sign telling them the natural monument is further on. It stands behind and to the left of the main hall: fifteen metres round, twenty-four metres tall, tied for the second-thickest tree in Shizuoka prefecture behind the camphor at Atami.

Published sources put it at a thousand years or more, which in Japan usually means tradition rather than a ring count, and this is no exception. The trunk can be measured, and has been twice. The Environment Ministry's giant-tree survey recorded fourteen metres of girth in 1990 and fifteen in 2001, ranking it nineteenth in the country and then thirty-second. The tree did not shrink; surveyors kept finding giants elsewhere.

Its two famous neighbours on the peninsula, at Atami and at Ito's Kuzumi-jinja, have both hollowed out. This one has not. It has dropped some large branches over the centuries and kept its trunk whole, which at this age and this girth is rare.

A national Natural Monument since December 1936.
trees.access: Free. Shrine grounds, open to visitors. A sign at the entrance points visitors past two smaller camphors near the torii and the main hall to the real monument tree further in ('the natural monument great camphor is further on').
trees.transport: Izu Kyuko Line to Kawazu Station, then about 12-15 minutes on foot (or a short bus ride from the station to the Kinomiyaguchi stop).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the third camphor you meet, past two smaller ones near the torii and a sign directing you on, 15 metres round. It stands behind and to the left of the main hall at Kawazu Kinomiya Shrine.

trees.access: Free (formerly a paid attraction, now open to the public at no charge). Stands on a plot Kawazu town has landscaped beside the Odoriko Onsen Kaikan bathhouse and nearby restaurants; free parking on site.
trees.transport: Izu Kyuko Line to Kawazu Station, then Tokai Bus toward Shuzenji Station, about 7 minutes to the Odoriko Onsen Kaikan stop, right there. About 60km / 90 minutes by car from the Numachi or Nagaizumi-Numazu expressway interchanges via the Izu-Judan Expressway and Route 414.
trees.story:
Four thick branches run along the ground from this cycad's base like the arms of something reaching rather than growing, described in Japanese sources as looking like a giant snake writhing. A central trunk rises about ten metres, unusually tall for a cycad, and the whole clump measures 7.76 metres around at the base, not a single trunk's girth but the combined mass of stem and limbs together.

Tradition places its age anywhere from six hundred to over a thousand years, tied to a story that the tree was already a splendid giant when O-Man, later a consort of Tokugawa Ieyasu and mother of the founders of the Kii and Mito Tokugawa branches, was born on this plot before 1607 to the Masaki family who owned the land. A fire damaged its eastern side in 1916; it recovered, and became a National Natural Monument in 1936, one of only ten individually designated cycads in the whole of Japan. Emperor Showa and Empress Kojun came to see it in June 1981.

Its vigour has declined somewhat in recent years, which the record should say plainly rather than smooth over. It stands a few minutes' walk from Kawazu Station, beside the Odoriko Onsen Kaikan bathhouse and about six hundred metres from the Great Camphor already mapped here, free to see, once a private garden and now a public plot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its shape, a low central trunk about ten metres tall with four thick branches sprawling along the ground in every direction. It stands beside the Odoriko Onsen Kaikan bathhouse.
